questions.prompt: Which four ingredients does Lesson 1 say every strong prompt needs to specify, so the model isn't left to guess at what you actually want?
options: Task, Context, Format, Constraints
Role, Tone, Length, Audience
Input, Output, Model, Temperature
Instructions, Examples, Rules, Format
Context, History, Retrieval, Memory
Task, Role, Schema, Budget
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines the four ingredients as Task (the exact action/deliverable), Context (who it's for and the situation), Format (the output's shape), and Constraints (tone, scope, things to avoid) — leaving any one unspecified forces the model to guess.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B's Role belongs to Lesson 3's system prompts, not Lesson 1's four core ingredients — the two lessons cover related but distinct ideas, and mixing them up here misses that Format and Constraints are the categories this specific lesson names.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the model picking up a pattern from examples included directly in the prompt, without any retraining, is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 2's key terms define in-context learning as the model picking up a pattern from examples in the prompt itself, without retraining — the mechanism that makes few-shot prompting work.

questions.prompt: A zero-shot support-ticket classifier gets the right category most of the time, but is specifically inconsistent on tickets that mention two issues at once (a charge and a bug). Per Lesson 2, what's the most targeted fix?
options: Add 2-5 few-shot examples that specifically demonstrate how to classify a ticket touching two categories at once
Rewrite the zero-shot instructions to be twice as long
Lower the model's temperature to zero
Switch to a completely different base model
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names inconsistent zero-shot results on a judgment call as exactly when few-shot earns its keep — a worked example showing how to resolve the dual-category case does what a longer plain-language description can't.

questions.prompt: Match each instruction to where Lesson 3 says it belongs: the system prompt or the user message.
left: "You are a support agent for Northwind Traders"
"For billing disputes, escalate to a human and stop there"
questions.explain: Role and hard boundaries/escalation rules belong in the system prompt because they apply to every turn; a specific question and a one-off request to change format just this once belong in the user message.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about prompt template variables, per Lesson 4.
options: A well-scoped variable holds exactly one piece of information that genuinely changes per call
A `{{instructions}}` variable filled with a different full paragraph of rules each call defeats the purpose of templating
The fixed, tested parts of a prompt — role, tone, format, constraints — should live in a variable, not the template itself
Two different fills of the same template should still produce output that follows the same structure and rules
A template needs at least five variables to be considered useful
questions.explain: A well-scoped variable holds one changing fact, and an `{{instructions}}`-style variable defeats templating by smuggling a whole new prompt back in. The fixed parts belong in the template itself, not a variable — and a working template should produce consistent structure across different fills, regardless of how many variables it has.

questions.prompt: Put Lesson 6's four-step prompt iteration loop in the order it's meant to run.
items: BASELINE — run the current prompt against a fixed set of test inputs and save the outputs
TEST CASES — pick inputs that cover typical, edge-case, and already-failing examples
ONE CHANGE — edit exactly one thing in the prompt
COMPARE — re-run the same test inputs and keep the change only if it actually helped
questions.explain: The loop establishes a baseline, picks test cases covering the real range of inputs, changes exactly one variable, then compares against the baseline — repeating for the next issue rather than tweaking and re-running on a vibe check.

questions.prompt: A prompt says: "Be extremely detailed, but keep your answer under 50 words." Which of Lesson 5's four failure modes is this?
options: Conflicting instructions
Ambiguous instructions
Missing output format
Prompt overloading
questions.explain: "Extremely detailed" and "under 50 words" can't both be true for most real topics, so the model has to silently pick a winner — Lesson 5's definition of conflicting instructions, not an ambiguous or missing-format problem.

questions.prompt: What does chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting ask the model to do?
options: Reason step by step before giving a final answer
Sample the same prompt multiple times and vote on the majority answer
Adopt a specific expert persona before answering
Return output in an exact, parseable JSON schema
Break one large task into a sequence of smaller prompts
Skip directly to the final answer without showing intermediate steps
questions.explain: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step before giving a final answer, giving it room to catch its own arithmetic or logical slips the way working a problem out on paper does.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes self-consistency (Lesson 8), a separate technique that samples chain-of-thought multiple times and votes — it builds on CoT but isn't what CoT itself is defined as.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: sampling the same chain-of-thought prompt multiple times, independently, and taking the answer that shows up most often across the runs is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 8 defines self-consistency as running the same CoT prompt several times and taking the majority answer, rather than trusting whichever single run came first.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about role-based prompting, per Lesson 9.
options: Assigning a role changes vocabulary and depth, not just tone
"Act like a doctor" is a stronger role prompt than specifying a board-certified pediatrician explaining a fever to a worried parent
A per-request role can be layered onto one task without changing the assistant's overall system-prompt identity
Role-based prompting always means permanently changing the application's system prompt
A one-word role gives the model a costume, not expertise
questions.explain: A role shifts vocabulary, priorities, and depth, and can be applied per-request without touching the system prompt's standing identity. A vague one-word role like "act like a doctor" is the weaker option, not the stronger one, since it specifies a costume instead of real expertise.

questions.prompt: A downstream service needs to parse a model's extracted name, email, and order-number output with code. Per Lesson 10, what's missing from a prompt that just says "Extract the name, email, and order number from this message"?
options: A concrete output schema shown in the prompt, plus an instruction like "return ONLY valid JSON, no other text"
A longer, more polite phrasing of the request
A request for the model to explain its extraction process first
A higher sampling temperature
questions.explain: Showing the model the exact shape to copy — not just describing the fields — plus closing off any preamble is what makes structured output reliably parseable run after run; politeness and temperature don't address the format gap at all.

questions.prompt: Match each technique from this chapter to its definition.
right: Breaking one large task into a sequence of smaller prompts, each feeding the next
Asking the model to return output in an exact, parseable shape
Asking the model to reason step by step before a final answer
Sampling the same prompt multiple times and taking the majority answer
questions.explain: Chain-of-thought asks for step-by-step reasoning; self-consistency samples a CoT prompt repeatedly and votes; prompt chaining splits one task into a sequence of smaller prompts; structured output prompting constrains the response to an exact, parseable shape.

questions.prompt: Put these three chain steps from Lesson 11's worked example in the order they run, turning a transcript into a translated executive summary.
items: Extract — pull every direct quote about pricing as a JSON array of strings
Summarize — condense the pricing quotes into 3 key themes, one sentence each
Translate — translate the 3-sentence summary into Spanish
questions.explain: Each step's output feeds the next: the extracted quotes are summarized into themes, and the resulting summary is what actually gets translated — reversing the order would leave the translation step with nothing usable to work from.

questions.prompt: A support bot's actual instruction — "refund this order" — is only 40 tokens, but the full API call sends nearly 13,000 tokens once tool schemas, history, and retrieved documents are included. When the bot answers wrong, what does Lesson 12 say to ask first?
options: Whether the problem is the one-line instruction itself, or something in the context surrounding it
Whether the model needs a larger context window
Whether the system prompt should be deleted entirely
Whether the user's wording needs to be more polite
questions.explain: Lesson 12's whole point is that "reword the prompt" and "fix what's being fed into the context window" are two different fixes — and only one of them addresses an answer that got buried under thousands of tokens of history and retrieved content.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a token budget worksheet, the tokens set aside for the model's response — subtracted first, before anything else — are called the ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 sets the output reserve aside first, before fixed costs or variable caps, because a response that gets cut off mid-sentence is a worse failure than trimming the input a bit more.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about managing a context window budget, per Lessons 13-14.
options: Conversation history and retrieved content both need an explicit cap, or either one can eventually consume the entire remaining budget
The system prompt and tool schemas are fixed costs that should be measured once and subtracted
Hitting a variable cost's cap means no new content can ever be added to that component again
Hitting a cap means it's time to shrink what's already there, which is what compression is for
~4 characters per token is a usable rule of thumb for estimating English text
questions.explain: History and retrieval both need caps or they'll eat the budget; fixed costs like the system prompt and tools are measured once. A cap being hit means shrink, not freeze — that's what Lesson 14's compression techniques are for — and ~4 characters per token is the stated rule of thumb.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 15's ordering recipe, put these pieces of an assembled context window in order from the start of the window to the end.
items: Top-ranked retrieved chunk (placed right before the question)
questions.explain: The recipe puts system rules and tool schemas in the strongest early position, lower-priority background in the weakest (middle) position, and reserves the strong end-of-window position for the single most relevant retrieved chunk placed right next to the question itself.

questions.prompt: A tool is defined with description: "Gets order info." Per Lesson 16, what's the real problem with this, independent of whether the model ever actually calls the tool?
options: It costs the same tokens on every call as a precise description would, while giving the model far less to work with
It will cause the API call to be rejected outright
It makes the tool free to call instead of metered
It automatically gets replaced by the model with a better description
questions.explain: Every tool schema offered is sent on every call regardless of use, so a vague description is the worst combination in a context budget: full token price, reduced value for deciding whether and how to call it.

questions.prompt: Match each fact to where Lesson 17 says it belongs: short-term memory or long-term memory.
left: A calculation being worked out in the current turn
A stated preference that should be remembered in future, unrelated sessions
A document the user just pasted into this conversation
A decision like "already declined the upsell twice" that should persist
questions.explain: Anything scoped to the current task — a calculation, a pasted document — can stay short-term and disappear with the session. A preference or decision worth keeping across unrelated future sessions needs long-term storage instead.

questions.prompt: A fact was retrieved, fits well within the token budget, and is genuinely present in the context — but the model's response still misses it, and the fact happened to sit in the dead center of a 50,000-token window. Per Lesson 15, what's the most likely explanation?
options: The "lost in the middle" effect — position in the window, not whether it fits, affected recall
The fact must have been compressed or cut, which is a budget problem
The retrieval step must have ranked the fact incorrectly
The model's context window must be too small for this fact
questions.explain: Since the fact is present and within budget, this isn't a budget or ranking problem — it's a position problem: content in the middle of a long context is recalled less reliably than content near the start or end, even when fully present.

questions.prompt: An eval set built only from easy, obviously-correct examples is, per Lesson 18, mostly useless for one specific reason. What is it?
options: It passes almost any reasonable prompt, so it can't catch a regression
It takes too long to run in an automated test loop
It requires an LLM-as-judge to grade every case
It can only be used once before needing to be deleted
questions.explain: An eval set that's all happy-path cases will pass nearly any reasonable prompt version, which means it can't distinguish a real improvement from a real regression — exactly why Lesson 18 requires edge, known-failure, and adversarial cases too.

questions.prompt: Select every grading method Lesson 19 names as a valid way to grade an eval case's output.
options: Exact or structural match
Keyword or regex assertions
LLM-as-judge rubric scoring
Human spot-check sampling
Running the prompt against a larger base model and comparing API costs
questions.explain: Lesson 19 names four grading methods: exact/structural match, keyword or regex assertions, LLM-as-judge rubric scoring, and human spot-check sampling to keep the automated judge honest. Comparing API costs against a different model isn't a grading method at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: using a second model to grade open-ended output against a written rubric is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 defines LLM-as-judge as a second model grading genuinely open-ended output — tone, helpfulness, clarity — against a written rubric, the only practical way to grade output with no single correct form.

questions.prompt: An A/B test changes a prompt's wording, tone, and output format all at once between the control and the challenger, then reports the challenger as the clear winner. Which of Lesson 20's four rules does this violate?
options: Change one variable at a time
Use the same eval set, or a fair traffic split, for both versions
Pick the metric in advance
Use a big-enough sample before shipping the winner
questions.explain: Changing wording, tone, and format simultaneously means a result in the challenger's favor can't be attributed to any one of those changes — or ruled out as one of them dragging the others down — which is exactly what isolating one variable at a time is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each grading scenario to the Lesson 19 grading method that fits it best.
left: Checking that an extracted field is valid JSON matching an exact schema
Checking that a reply never leaks an internal system detail
Scoring whether an open-ended explanation is actually clear
Periodically catching a drifting or biased automated judge
questions.explain: A schema check is exact/structural match; a never-leak check is a keyword/regex assertion; open-ended clarity needs LLM-as-judge rubric scoring; and catching a drifting judge is exactly what periodic human spot-checking is for.

questions.prompt: Version v15 of a prompt has a higher overall pass rate than v14, but one case that passed on v14 now fails on v15. Per Lesson 21, how should this be treated?
options: As a blocking regression, regardless of the higher overall pass rate
As a non-issue, since the overall pass rate improved
As proof the eval set needs that case removed
As evidence v14 should be restored permanently
questions.explain: Regression testing answers "did anything that used to work stop working," not "is this version better overall" — a pass-to-fail flip is flagged and blocks shipping regardless of what happened to the aggregate pass rate.

questions.prompt: Per the capstone brief in Lesson 22, in what order should its deliverables actually be built?
options: Working prompts first, then the context budget and ordering, then the eval set and automated testing, then the A/B comparison and regression baseline
The regression baseline first, so there's something to compare every later step against
The eval set first, before any prompt exists to test against it
All ten deliverables at once, since none of them depend on each other
questions.explain: Lesson 22's realistic order gets the use case and prompts working first, adds the context budget and ordering once that works, builds the eval set and runs automated testing once there's a stable combination to measure, and only then runs the A/B comparison and sets the regression baseline — each stage needs the one before it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23, what turns a folder of prompt files into an actual library — rather than just a folder — is the ________, a dated version history connecting each prompt version to its actual eval results.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 names CHANGELOG.md as the piece that makes the difference: a dated history linking each version of the prompt to a real score, so a change can be justified by evidence instead of a feeling that it "seems better."

questions.prompt: Put Lesson 23's build order for the capstone prompt library in sequence.
items: Write system.md and the task-specific templates
Build eval_set.json with at least 10 real cases across all four categories
Run automated tests and log a dated entry in CHANGELOG.md
questions.explain: The prompts have to work before there's anything to budget or test; the budget and tool descriptions get written down once that's stable; the eval set is built against how the prompts actually behave; and only then does a real test run produce a score worth logging in the changelog.

questions.prompt: Lesson 24 says a live automated test run, performed in front of whoever you're presenting to, is worth more than a pass rate you remember from last week. Why?
options: A number generated live is proof; a number recalled from memory is just a claim
Live test runs are always faster to execute than ones run in advance
A live run is the only way to produce a pass rate at all
Presenting the test live is a requirement for receiving a course certificate
questions.explain: The distinction Lesson 24 draws is evidentiary: a number you generate on the spot, in front of the reviewer, is verifiable proof, while the same number recited from memory is an unverified claim — the whole point of building a real, running prompt library instead of describing one.
